1.pericope_label: The words of the covenant in the land of Moab

schools.summary: Gill takes the words of the covenant to point forward rather than back — not to what goes before, but to what follows in the next chapters to the end of the book, where promises of grace and of good things to Jews and Gentiles are intermixed with other matter.

Henry takes the renewal itself for the lesson. Moses, who was mediator before, is mediator still, and yet even Moses, king in Jeshurun though he was, could make the covenant no otherwise than as God gave him instructions: it does not lie in the power of ministers to fix the terms of the covenant, they are only to dispense the seals of it. He observes that this is called a covenant besides the one made in Horeb because, though the covenant was the same, this was a new promulgation and ratification of it; that some then living had been old enough to consent for themselves at Horeb and are brought into it again, since those who have solemnly covenanted with God should take all opportunities to do it afresh, as those that like their choice too well to change; and that the far greater part were a new generation, so that it is fit the covenant should be renewed to the children of the covenant.

Clarke holds that this verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter, since a widely different subject is taken up at the second verse, and notes that it is numbered as the sixty-ninth verse in some of the most correct copies of the Hebrew Bible. He supplies the force of the verb rendered make, lichroth, to cut, alluding to the covenant sacrifice offered on such an occasion and divided; and he holds what is instituted here to be an addition to the ten words given at Horeb, the curses denounced in this chapter differing from those denounced against transgressors of the decalogue. Wesley reads the opening as naming the terms or conditions on which God renewed his covenant with them, and states the relation between the two in a line: the covenant was but one in substance, though various in the time and manner of its dispensation.

Ellicott rejects the arrangement Clarke accepts. The Hebrew Bibles do add this verse to the previous chapter and begin the new one at the second verse, but they cannot be right in so doing; the pronoun in Hebrew has nothing in it to determine whether it looks backward or forward, and the context settles the matter, since the covenant is described in the chapter that follows. He then finds a larger significance in where the chapter stands: this covenant in the land of Moab lies outside the tremendous sanction appended to the expansion of the Sinaitic covenant, much as the chapter on vows in Leviticus lies outside the sanction preceding it, vows not being compulsory; so that the curse is not the end of God's dealings with the chosen people, and after it there is still another covenant to the force of which there is no limit. Keil describes the transaction more soberly, as a renewed declaration of the covenant concluded at Horeb, or a fresh obligation to keep it, no repetition of the sacrificial act being necessary because the covenant had never been abrogated on God's part.

debates.question: Does this verse close the preceding chapter or open this one?

positions.position: it belongs to the preceding chapter, and is numbered as its sixty-ninth verse in the best Hebrew copies
the Hebrew Bibles cannot be right in so dividing it; the context shows the covenant is described in what follows
the words point forward, to what follows to the end of the book

outliers.note: argues from the chapter's position that the Sinaitic curse is not God's last word — after it stands a covenant with no limit to its force, and nothing can destroy the relation between the Lord and Israel

themes: a covenant renewed rather than replaced
where the chapter begins
the curse is not the end of God’s dealings

2.pericope_label: The recital: what your eyes have seen, and the heart not yet given

schools.summary: Gill notes that Moses had been speaking to the heads of the people and now summoned the whole body, a solemn covenant being about to be made; he reads the great temptations as the ten plagues, which tried the Egyptians whether they would let Israel go and tried the Israelites whether they would trust God's power to deliver them; and on the heart not given he distinguishes seeing with the bodily eye from discerning with the eye of the understanding, citing Jarchi for a heart to know the mercies of the Lord and to cleave to him. Calvin refers the whole recital to the preface of the Law, since its tendency is to recommend the Law and prepare the people to be teachable, and holds that it would have been the height of baseness not to devote themselves to a Deliverer who had dealt so graciously with them. On the sentence itself his figure is the drunken man, or one in a lethargy, who hears a cry and raises his head a moment and opens his eyes, and then relapses into torpor. A clear and powerful understanding is a special gift of the Spirit, since men are ever blind even in the brightest light until God enlightens them; and yet the defect does not free us from blame, since every man's conscience convicts him that his ignorance is bound up with pride and indolence and is therefore voluntary.

Clarke reports that some critics read the fourth verse interrogatively, and hath not God given you a heart, on the ground that God could not reprehend them for failing in a duty when he had given them neither mind nor strength for it. The point is strictly just, he allows, but the interrogation is unnecessary: the words imply only that they had not such a heart, not because God withheld the means of knowledge or the helps of his grace, but because they had not faithfully used them; had they had such a heart it would have been God's gift, for he is the author of all good, and that they had it not is proof they had grieved his Spirit. On the wilderness provision he states the principle plainly, that they were not supported in an ordinary providential way but by continual miracle, and that the means were ineffectual not because they were ill-calculated to answer God's purpose but because the people were not workers with him. Wesley reaches the same balance: their want of grace was their own fault and the just punishment of former sins, as with the men of Isaiah's day who first shut their own eyes and then had them closed by the righteous judgment of God.

Ellicott compares the address with Joshua's to the people as distinct from their heads and officers, notes how few the topics are — the miracles of the Exodus, the wilderness journey, the conquest of Sihon and Og — and marks the emphatic pronoun: yourselves are the witnesses, I need not repeat the story. Every rank is summoned, from the captains of the tribes to the little ones and the lowest slaves, and the point set before them is one simple thing, to accept the Lord as their God. He quotes Rashi on the heart not given, a heart to mark the mercies of the Holy One and to cleave unto him, and catches the detail no one else does — that they drank neither wine nor strong drink is a fact stated here only, and evidently comes from the lips of one who knew their walking through the wilderness. Keil reads all Israel as the nation in all its members, and takes the complaint about the heart not as an excuse for the past want of susceptibility but as an explanation of why the gracious acts of God have to be rehearsed again and laid to heart.

debates.question: How can God reproach them for lacking a heart he had not given?

positions.position: read the clause as a question — and has God not given you a heart? — since he could not reprehend a duty he gave no power to perform
no interrogation is needed: the means and helps were given and not faithfully used, which is proof his Spirit had been grieved
understanding is a special gift of the Spirit and men are blind until enlightened, yet the defect remains voluntary and blameable

outliers.note: declines to read the verse as either excuse or accusation, taking it instead as Moses' reason for rehearsing the same mercies yet again

themes: seeing with the eye and not with the understanding
grace withheld, or grace unused
the provision of the forty years

10.pericope_label: Ye stand this day all of you

schools.summary: Gill places them at the door of the tabernacle at the summons of Moses, or as Aben Ezra has it round about the ark, the symbol of the divine presence. Calvin descends the same ladder of parties that Henry does, from the officers and elders and heads of families down to the little children and the wives, and adds the very porters and baggage-carriers, so that the minds of those who derived their origin from the holy patriarchs should be the more solemnly impressed. He presses the oath from the human side — if perjury between man and man is detestable, much less pardonable is it to belie what you have promised God by his sacred name — and adds an argument from antiquity, that God had prevented them by his grace many ages before they were born. He then raises the hard question himself: how could the little children pass into covenant, not being of an age to learn what it contained? Though they did not receive the promised salvation by faith, nor renounce the flesh so as to dedicate themselves, they were bound by the same obligations their parents laid themselves under, since the grace was common to all; circumcision was the sign of that adoption from the mother's womb, and infants are now initiated by baptism into the service of a God they do not yet know, because he claims them as his children when he engrafts them into the body of Christ.

Henry walks the list of parties from top to bottom. The great men must not think it any disparagement to their honour or diminution of their power to put their necks under the yoke of this covenant; rather they must enter first, to set a good example to their inferiors. The wives and children come in though they were never numbered or mustered, for even little ones are capable of being taken into covenant with God and are to be admitted with their parents. The stranger comes in, provided he had renounced all false gods, which Henry reads as an early indication of favour to the Gentiles. And the hewers of wood and drawers of water come in, the meanest drudges among them: as none are too great to come under the bonds of the covenant, so none are too mean to inherit its blessings. On the oath he hears God speaking — it is his oath, he has drawn it up and settled it, he has sworn to you and to him you must be sworn — which requires us to be sincere and serious, humble and reverent in our covenant transactions with him.
Clarke gives the reason for the staging: a covenant implies two contracting parties, so God is represented as present while they and all their families, old and young, come before him.

Keil reads the summons as one to enter inwardly, to make the covenant an affair of the heart and life, and notes that on that day the whole nation stood there without a single exception. He also corrects the rendering: the two members of the sentence are parallel, the heads of the people being the elders and officers and the tribes consisting of all the men, so that the Greek and Syriac reading, captains of your tribes, is at variance with the language. Ellicott needs one sentence for the point of it — there is no limit to the blessing of following the Lord and keeping his word, and it is open to all, from the highest to the lowest, to take hold of his covenant.

debates.question: How could little children enter a covenant they were too young to understand?

positions.position: they were bound by the obligations their parents laid themselves under, the grace being common to all; circumcision sealed the adoption before faith or understanding, as baptism does now
even little ones are capable of being taken into covenant with God and are to be admitted with their parents

outliers.note: rejects the Greek and Syriac 'captains of your tribes' as against the language, reading the two clauses as parallel — heads and tribes, elders and officers, all the men of Israel

themes: none too great and none too mean for the covenant
the covenant confirmed by an oath
how infants can be bound by it

11.pericope_label: Who enters the covenant, and what passing into it means

schools.summary: Gill notices what is unusual in the list before explaining anything: the little ones and the wives are scarce ever mentioned in any special law or solemn transaction, and here they stand named. On the verb he reports the rabbinic view, from Jarchi and Aben Ezra, that to pass into covenant alludes to the manner of making covenants by slaying a creature, cutting it in pieces, and passing between them; and he reads the establishing of a people as containing the sum and substance of the whole covenant.

Clarke sets out the old covenant rite in full, as seven particulars: the contracting parties, hitherto separate, agree to enter a state of close and permanent amity; they meet in solemn assembly; a sacrifice is offered to God, the whole being a religious act; the victim is divided into two equal parts along the spine and the parts laid opposite each other with room between; the parties meet in the victim; the conditions are recited; and an oath is taken by which the covenant is made and ratified. Wesley states the object of the oath in a line, that they entered into covenant confirmed by a solemn oath, and takes the establishing of a people as the summary of the whole: that they should be established for a people to him, to fear and love and obey and be devoted to him, and that he should be to them a God, to make them holy and happy — a due sense of which relation is enough to bring us to all the duties and all the comforts of the covenant.

Ellicott reaches for both ends of the covenant's history: behind this stands the promise to Abraham that the Almighty would be a God to him and to his seed, taking in the child of eight days old and the slave, who were to receive the sign in their flesh; ahead of it stand Peter's words at Pentecost, that the promise is unto you and to your children. From the hewer of wood he passes on Rashi's inference that there were Canaanites who became proselytes in the time of Moses, as the Gibeonites did in the days of Joshua. On the verb he is more cautious than the others: Rashi illustrates it by the passing between the parts of a divided victim, but no such ceremony is mentioned here, and we can only say that the practice may possibly have given occasion for this use of the word. His weightiest note is on the covenant's direction — this is the aspect of it which makes the Lord responsible for the fulfilment of the whole, the people's part being only to accept the position, which brings it into the closest similarity with the new covenant, whose form is that I will be to them a God and they shall be to me a people. Keil defines the idiom, that to pass into a covenant expresses entire entrance, going completely through the territory entered, and is more emphatic than the commoner phrase for coming into one.

debates.question: Does 'pass into the covenant' allude to passing between the parts of a divided victim?

positions.position: yes — it is the old rite of the covenant sacrifice, cut in pieces with the parties passing between
no such ceremony is mentioned here; at most the practice may have given occasion for this use of the word

outliers.note: reads the thirteenth verse as making God responsible for the fulfilment of both halves of the covenant, and so as the nearest thing in the Law to the new covenant of the prophets

themes: what it means to pass into a covenant
the covenant that includes the powerless
God undertaking for both parties

14.pericope_label: Not with you only: the absent, the unborn, and the idols they had seen

schools.summary: Gill gives Aben Ezra's reading of the clause, not only you but those that will come after you, your sons and your sons' sons, and counts the years behind the warning — upwards of two hundred in a country much given to idolatry, where they had seen many of its idols and much of its worship, so that their hearts had been apt to be ensnared and some minds tinctured with it, and the remembrance might yet make ill impressions on them. Calvin looks forward rather than back. We know how greatly men's minds are tickled by novelty, and on entering Canaan they would meet many forms of idolatry hitherto unknown, so many snares to entangle them; so Moses exhorts them to beware by former instances, since they knew by extraordinary proofs that whatever imaginations the heathen nations had invented were hateful to God. The argument, he says, is drawn from experience.

Clarke states the scope of the clause in a line: him that standeth here is the present generation, him that is not here is all future generations of this people. Wesley works the same point out by an argument from ordinary law. The covenant was made at first with Abraham and his seed, and as God engaged himself to continue the blessing of Abraham upon his posterity, so he engaged them to the same duties required of Abraham; and so it is even among men, where a king confers an estate upon a subject and his heirs for ever upon certain conditions, all his heirs who enjoy that benefit being obliged to the same conditions. He allows that the phrase may take in those constrained to be absent by sickness or necessary occasion, and reports the boldest reading of all, from one of the Chaldee paraphrasts, that all the generations that have been from the first days of the world and all that shall arise to the end of the whole world stand with us here this day. Taking the transaction as a typical dispensation of the covenant of grace, he finds in that a noble testimony to the Mediator of it, who is the same yesterday, today and for ever. On Egypt he is blunt: they had learned too much of those idolatries, as the golden calf shewed, and there also they were in dreadful bondage, whence God alone delivered them.

Keil widens the clause further than either. The covenant was made with all, whether present or not, and was to embrace not only those living then but their descendants, so as to become a covenant of blessing for all nations — which is why he hears behind it both Peter's promise to you and to your children and the intercession of Christ for those who should believe through the apostles' word. He reads the appeal to Egypt as the opening of an exposition of the evil results of apostasy, resting on what the people had learned by experience of the worthlessness of idols: that they are not gods at all but only wood and stone, gillulim, a word meaning literally clods.

outliers.note: argues the point from inheritance law — a king granting an estate to a subject and his heirs binds every heir who enjoys it to the same conditions — and then quotes a Chaldee paraphrast who has every generation from the world's first days to its last standing present at Moab

themes: the covenant binding on the absent and the unborn
idolatry learned in Egypt and met again in Canaan
idols as wood and stone

17.pericope_label: The root that beareth gall and wormwood

schools.summary: Gill will not let the word for idols pass politely: it has the signification of dung, and may be rendered dunghill gods, either because some were bred and lived in dung, as Bishop Patrick says of the beetle the Egyptians worshipped, or simply because they were as loathsome as dung. He reads the man who blesses himself as hardhearted, impenitent and obstinate, and guilty of the grossest and most provoking of sins. Calvin reads the root as something more interior, understanding by the word the hidden principles of sins, which unless prevented in good time spring up with collected vigour and lift themselves on high, since indulgence in sin increases by concealment and connivance; and he notices that Moses passes from man and woman to family and tribe, so that those associated with others in sin excuse themselves in vain by their numbers, a whole nation being as much to be condemned as a single person. On the self-blessing he is sharper still: to bless oneself is to hope in one's secret imaginations that all will go well, as hypocrites do, who in their foolish self-adulation applaud themselves deceitfully lest they should hear God thundering; and nothing is worse than to hope for peace while we wage war with God. He takes the last clause of the verse by a proverbial figure, that Moses forbids us to excite appetites already heated by new stimulants, as those do who add oil to a fire already lit, lust in a man being like an insatiable dropsy; and he holds that the obstinacy in which the wicked are wilfully hardened shuts against them the door of hope, since the man who abandons himself to sin expecting impunity has not only extinguished the light of his own reason but dethroned God, as if he were not the Judge of the world.

Clarke identifies the root with the apostle's evil heart of unbelief departing from the living God, allowing that it may mean false doctrines or idolatrous persons too, and reads the closing proverb as denoting the utmost indulgence in all sensual gratifications. Wesley defines the root as an evil heart inclining them to cursed idolatry and bringing forth bitter fruits, and puts the self-deception plainly: the man flatters himself in his own eyes with vain hopes, as if God did not mind such things and either could not or would not punish them. He would reverse the last clause and read it as adding thirst to drunkenness — when the man has multiplied his sins and made himself as it were drunk with them he is still not satisfied, but whets his appetite for more, as drunkards contrive to make themselves thirsty again. On the sentence he notes that the man is separated unto some peculiar and exemplary plague, made a monument of God's displeasure to the whole land.

Keil supplies the botany of the image: rosh is a plant of very bitter taste, commonly coupled with wormwood, and though not strictly poisonous it makes a striking image of the destructive fruit borne by idolatry. Ellicott sets the clause in the chapter's argument — I make this covenant binding upon all your generations in case there should even now be some root of idolatry among you which may bear fruit in later times and bring a curse upon the country — and observes that there were such roots is only too plain from what followed after the elders of that generation died. He corrects the word that carries the self-blessing, which is not the imagination of the heart but the stubbornness of it, and records a third reading of the closing proverb, from the Greek, which turns it into a plea: that one idolater would not make much difference to Israel, that the drunkard could not be the ruin of the thirsty, and so a man might do as he pleased and escape punishment, protected by the general prosperity of the nation — a mistaken view which the warning in Hebrews meets admirably. On the sentence he hears the verdict in the verbs, the anger that shall smoke as Sinai was altogether on a smoke when the Lord descended in fire, and the curses that shall lie upon the man as beasts lie down in their lairs.

positions.position: to excite appetites already heated by new stimulants, as men add oil to a fire already lit
the reverse — having made himself drunk with sin he whets his appetite for more, as drunkards contrive to make themselves thirsty again
on the Greek reading, a plea that one sinner cannot ruin the nation and may therefore escape under its general prosperity

outliers.note: reads the root not as a person but as the concealed principle of sin itself, which grows precisely because it is hidden — indulgence increasing by connivance

themes: the hidden root and its bitter fruit
the man who blesses himself in his heart
adding drunkenness to thirst

22.pericope_label: What the nations will ask, and what they will be told

schools.summary: Gill dates the asking late, not to the next generation but to future ages, even after the destruction of Judea by the Romans, and hears the rooting out as fulfilled twice over, at the Babylonish captivity and again by the Romans; he marks the difference between them, that at the end of seventy years they returned from Babylon, whereas from the later dispersion, he writes, they have not been able to return these seventeen hundred years. Calvin explains why the question gets asked at all. The punishments would be no ordinary ones, such as fall into contempt from their common use, but like portents; and the question refers to something extraordinary and not easily comprehended, looking back over the whole list of curses, not that each by itself would awaken such horror, but that heaped one upon another, by their number and severity and duration, they compelled men to wonder. Everywhere men are afflicted with diseases, and barrenness for a season is a common evil; but that sickness should cleave as it were to the marrow of a whole people, and the earth be dried up as if burnt with sulphur, is an awful spectacle in which God's vengeance, which else would be incredible, manifestly appears. He notes too that strangers are introduced making the inquiry, so that the vengeance would be terrible even to heathen nations, and that Moses amplifies the crime: forsaking the God of their fathers, their deliverer, who had covenanted with them, they served strange and unknown gods from whom they had received no benefit, so that there could be no pretence of ignorance.

Henry states the moral and then refuses to leave the chapter where it ends. Idolatry would be the ruin of their nation; it is no new thing for God to bring desolating judgments on a people near to him in profession, and he never does it without good reason, so that it concerns us to seek the reason, that we may give glory to God and take warning to ourselves. But the law of Moses leaves sinners under the curse and rooted out of the Lord's land, whereas the grace of Christ toward penitent, believing sinners plants them again in their land, and they shall no more be pulled up, being kept by the power of God.

Clarke calls the phrase rendered gods whom he had not given unto them an unhappy translation, and will accept neither Houbigant's gods with whom they had no society nor Le Clerc's gods from whom they had received no benefit. The word signifies a portion, lot or inheritance, and God is frequently represented in scripture as the portion of his people; so the line should read that there was no portion to them — the gods they served could neither supply their wants nor save their souls. Wesley keeps the received rendering and finds another meaning in it: God had not given those gods to Israel for their worship, but had divided them unto all nations for their use and service, the reference being to the sun and moon and stars, which were the principal gods of the neighbouring nations.

Ellicott sets the two descriptions of the land side by side and lets them do the work — can this be the same country of which it was written that it is a land of brooks of water, of wheat and barley and vines, a land the Lord thy God careth for? Everyone knows which description has been nearer the fact for many centuries. He notes that Israel is represented as asking the same question in Jeremiah, compares the warning given to Solomon after the Temple was finished, and arrives independently at Clarke's sense of the disputed phrase, that none of those gods gave the people any portion. Keil reads the reply as ending in submission rather than explanation, closing with the confession that what is hidden belongs to the Lord and what is revealed to us and to our children, and takes the hidden to mean the manner in which God will yet carry out his purpose and complete his work of salvation notwithstanding the apostasy of the people.

debates.question: What does 'gods whom he had not given unto them' mean?

positions.position: the rendering is unhappy; the word means portion, and the sense is that those gods were no portion to them — unable to supply their wants or save their souls
God had not assigned those gods to Israel for worship, but divided them to all nations for use and service — the sun, moon and stars

outliers.note: reads the rooting out as fulfilled twice, and contrasts the seventy years of Babylon with a dispersion he dates, from his own century, at seventeen hundred years and still unended

themes: the desolation that makes strangers ask
gods who were no portion
the curse is not the last word

29.pericope_label: The secret things and the things revealed

schools.summary: Gill fills in what the hidden things are: much in nature that finite minds cannot account for, much in providence past finding out, especially the true causes and reasons of it, and much in God himself that revelation has not opened — not only perfections such as eternity and immensity, but the mode of subsistence of the three Persons in the Godhead. Calvin clears two readings away before offering his own. He rejects Aben Ezra's, that secret sins belong to God to punish while sins publicly done belong to men to punish, as forced, since punishment is not the subject here and Moses is commending the use of the doctrine of the Law; and he rejects the reading that makes the verse praise the Law for revealing God's secret things, since the demonstrative prefix on both clauses and the copula between them forbid running them together. His own takes the copula adversatively: God indeed retains to himself secret things, which it neither concerns nor profits us to know, but what he has declared belongs to us and to our children. He calls it a remarkable passage, condemning audacity and curiosity while rousing pious minds to seek instruction, since men are anxious to understand what it is unprofitable and even injurious to investigate, and all would be God's counsellors and penetrate the deepest recesses of heaven, while what God plainly sets before us is neglected or turned from in disgust.

Henry sets the ending beside Paul's, who closed his discourse on the same subject when it had begun to be fulfilled. We are forbidden curiously to inquire into the secret counsels of God, but directed and encouraged diligently to seek into what he has made known; he has kept back nothing profitable for us, but only that of which it is good for us to be ignorant. The end of all divine revelation is not to furnish curious subjects of speculation and discourse, but that we may do all the words of this law and be blessed in our deed; by this light a man may live and die comfortably, and be happy for ever.

Clarke rejects Houbigant's rendering, that the things hidden with the Lord are made manifest to us and our children for many generations, finding that none of the ancient versions understood it so. His own sense is that what God has thought proper to reveal is essential to the well-being of man and intended not for one time or one people but for all succeeding generations, while what he has not revealed concerns God alone and is not to be inquired after; he allows too that the words may refer to the subject of these chapters, since when a national apostasy may take place is known only to God. He notes that the Jews have always held these words of the highest importance, affixing marks in the original to the phrase to us and to our children. Wesley reads the exclamation as pastoral rather than doctrinal, spoken either to bridle a curiosity that would ask the time and manner of so great a judgment, or to quiet those who, seeing God deal so severely with his own people while sparing nations guilty of grosser idolatry, might take occasion to deny his providence or question the equity of his proceedings.

Ellicott admits that the immediate connection of the words with their context is not clear. He records Rashi's answer, which ties the secret things to the secret idolater earlier in the chapter — wilt thou punish the many for the devices of one, when no man knows the secrets of his fellow? — but finds more behind the passage than that. Moses was delivering not law only but prophecy, and there was more in this part of it than he himself could understand; must he not have longed to know what would befall his people in the latter days? All those curses were to come upon Israel, and after them there was still a covenant embracing every generation to the world's end; and if we, upon whom the ends of the world are come, do not yet see Israel's future distinctly, the words are appropriate still.

an adversative: God keeps to himself what it does not profit us to know, while what he has declared belongs to us and our children
on Rashi's reading, the secret idolater's heart is God's to reckon with, while what comes to light is ours to purge

outliers.note: takes the verse as Moses' own confessed horizon — a prophecy whose speaker could not see its end, and which still outruns its readers

themes: the bounds of lawful inquiry
revelation given that it may be done
a prophecy its own prophet could not read
